title: Scaleup surge latency vs cost concordance — platform notes
content:
Summary:

This is an internal sketch capturing a set of small-bench experiments and qualitative observations about how autoscaler-driven scaleups (rapid addition of slots/GPUs) correlate with latency percentile behavior and short-term cost spikes. The goal: produce a pragmatic set of heuristics we can embed in the autoscaler and guidance for product teams about expected cost vs tail-latency during business-critical bursts.

Motivation / context:
- Many docs look at steady-state cost/latency; fewer examine the transient window when capacity is added (scaleup).
- We saw multiple customer incidents where p95/p99 spiked despite low average CPU/GPU utilization because of queue reshuffling, KV-cache misses, and slot packing.
- Need a concise mapping: "If you increase capacity by X% over baseline within Y seconds, expect p99 to change by Z ms and unit cost to jump by Q%."

Experiment setup (short):
- Cluster: 8x H100 (shared pool) + simulated cold GPU pool (0 -> N) in k8s; small A/B with A100 for one run.
- Workloads: three synthetic mixes: 
  1) Text-only short (avg 80 tokens, seq 128) — conversational assistant emulation
  2) Multimodal mix (20% images->embedding, 80% text gen) — image+caption flows
  3) Stateful sessions (KV-cache heavy typical chat history)
- Traffic pattern: ramp 1 -> 400 qps over 30s (burst), hold 60s, ramp down. Repeat 6 times.
- Autoscaler: two policies tested: fast (add slots aggressively, target fill 90% within 10s) and conservative (gradual, target fill 90% within 60s).
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency (ms), cost estimate for that minute (dollars computed from GPU-minute + amortized infra), cache hit rate, queue depth, number of new workers created.

Representative numeric snapshots (text chart):
- For readability we report deltas vs baseline (baseline = steady-state pre-burst).

Run A (text-only, H100, fast autoscale):
- baseline: p50=40ms, p95=120ms, p99=240ms, cost/min=$0.55
- burst peak (t=18s, autoscale kicked): p50=45ms (+12%), p95=420ms (+250%), p99=980ms (+308%), cost/min=$1.30 (+136%)
- recovery (t=65s): p50=42ms, p95=140ms, p99=260ms, cost/min=$0.80

Run B (multimodal, H100, fast autoscale):
- baseline: p50=65ms, p95=260ms, p99=620ms, cost/min=$0.85
- burst peak: p50=78ms (+20%), p95=920ms (+254%), p99=2100ms (+239%) — large tail blowup due to synchronous image embedding warmups and blocking scheduling
- cost/min=$2.75 (+223%) during initial 30s as additional GPUs spun up and ran cold kernels with poor utilization

Run C (stateful / KV-heavy, H100, conservative autoscale):
- baseline: p50=38ms, p95=95ms, p99=170ms, cost/min=$0.60
- burst peak: p50=55ms (+45%), p95=180ms (+89%), p99=430ms (+153%), cost/min=$1.10 (+83%)
- observation: conservative ramp produced lower cost spike but longer sustained p95 elevation while caches re-warmed gradually

Small ASCII table (deltas vs baseline):

| Run | Autoscale | p95 delta | p99 delta | cost delta |
|-----|-----------|-----------:|----------:|-----------:|
| A   | fast      | +250%     | +308%     | +136%      |
| B   | fast      | +254%     | +239%     | +223%      |
| C   | conservative | +89%   | +153%     | +83%       |
Key observations / hypotheses:
1) Tail amplification mechanism: when new workers are created they often begin with empty KV caches and require kernel cold-paths (quantization fallback/kernels that instantiate slower memory paths). During the instantiation window many requests queue or contend on I/O leading to p99 blowups.
2) Multimodal workloads amplify the problem because image embedding operations can be CPU/GPU bursts that block shared scheduling, leading to head-of-line blocking for text streams.
3) Fast autoscale reduces average queue depth but increases the probability of seeing many cold workers concurrently, which can create a larger instantaneous cost spike and worse p99 compared to a more staggered approach.
4) Conservative autoscale trades cost spike magnitude for longer elevated tail latency while caches and kernel warmups complete.
5) Cost accounting (per-minute granularity) underestimates very short duration spikes; per-second accounting reveals true transient cost-to-latency concordance.

Practical heuristics we can add to autoscaler and platform docs:
- Autoscaler mode: provide a third hybrid ramp policy that staggers worker bootstrap by 200–500ms windows when burst size > 3x baseline; reduces simultaneous cold-kernel churn.
- Prefetching: for multimodal flows, pre-warm embedding kernels on a small warm pool (1–2 GPUs) when image requests are expected (predictive warmers based on route signature).
- KV-cache priming: maintain LRU cache snapshots that can be cloned to new workers to reduce cache miss storm on scale-up. Tradeoff: snapshot size vs copy time.
- Billing feedback: emit a short-lived "scaleup surcharge" metric (per-request) so product teams can see immediate cost impact of burst patterns.

Suggested quick wins (low dev time):
- Implement 250ms stagger on worker creation for bursts > 2x (infra change, low risk).
- Add per-second cost telemetry to existing cost dashboards (console change).
- Pilot a mini warm pool for multimodal routes (config flag per route).
- Create a small internal runbook for customer-facing SREs explaining expected p99 vs cost tradeoffs when customers plan marketing spikes.

Open questions / experiments to run next:
- Quantify the benefit of KV-snapshot cloning vs cache-warmth achieved by request pre-routing (A/B: clone-on-create vs shadow-traffic prefill).
- Measure delta for H100 vs A100 for image embedding cold kernel startup — we saw differences in absolute ms but need more runs for statistical confidence.
- Explore whether lower-precision kernel variants (fp16/q8) consistently reduce cold-start time at the cost of slight accuracy changes; measure tradeoffs.
- Estimate how much of the cost spike is billing granularity artifact vs real GPU runtime (cloud billing rounding practices).

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Attach the raw Prometheus scrape and the cost CSVs to the PLAT-1123 ticket.
- Run repeat experiments with 10 repeats and capture variance bands.
- Draft a one-pager for Product (optimize team) on route-level warm pools and suggested pricing guidance.

Appendix: short timeline narrative (example):
- 00:00–00:18: ramp begins, queue grows, first autoscale wave spawns 3 workers concurrently -> p95 spikes as KV misses occur
- 00:18–00:30: second wave spawns 5 workers to reach desired capacity; due to simultaneous kernel init, p99 jumps sharply; GPUs run at 40–55% utilization while expensive initialization happens
- 00:30–00:60: user-perceived latency stabilizes as KV caches warm and kernels JIT paths finish; cost remains elevated while new GPUs are billed for the minute

Bottom line (for exec / product):
- There is a clear concordance between scaleup policy, transient cost noise, and tail-latency. Fast scaleups reduce average queueing but can create larger transient tails and higher instantaneous cost. Conservative ramps reduce instant cost but extend the period of elevated latency. We should ship staggered boot, per-second cost telemetry, and a multimodal warm-pool feature as the three highest-impact items.
